title: Baseline documentation and pre-teardown diagnostics
notes: Do this BEFORE you touch a bolt. Everything you learn here changes the parts list. Pull DME data with Durametric/PIWIS/Autologic: record over-rev ranges (range 4-6 counts are the ones that matter), long/short term fuel trims, both bank O2 activity, and above all the camshaft deviation values for bank 1 and bank 2 — deviation beyond roughly +/-6 deg is the classic worn chain-ramp signature on an M96. Photograph the engine bay from every angle with the decklid open, and shoot close-ups of every connector, ground strap, vacuum line and hose clamp orientation. You will not remember how the AOS hoses route. Label connectors with numbered tape as you go. Record the engine number stamped on the lower edge of the crankcase near the sump flange — it is the only reliable way to pin down IMS variant and case casting.

children.title: Cut the oil filter and drop the sump plate for debris forensics
children.notes: This is the single highest-information-per-hour task in the whole job. Cut the filter open with a filter cutter and spread the pleats on a white shop towel. Fine glittery ferrous paste on a magnet = IMS bearing wearing out. Shiny non-ferrous aluminium flake = bore scoring or piston skirt material. Brass/copper = bearing shells. Black rubbery chunks = chain ramp/guide plastic. Photograph the pleats and photograph the magnetic drain plug. Keep the debris in a labelled bag — it is your evidence for what the teardown should focus on.

torque.note: Always use a new aluminium crush washer. A magnetic drain plug is a worthwhile permanent upgrade.
New cap O-ring every time.

children.title: Borescope all six cylinders through the spark plug holes
children.notes: Rotate the engine so each piston is at BDC and look at the thrust face of the bore. CRITICAL M96 CAVEAT: bore scoring starts at the BOTTOM of the cylinder and is hidden by the piston through most of its travel, so a clean borescope is NOT proof of a clean bore — only teardown is. Look for vertical score lines on the thrust side. On 996/997 the failure is reported more often on the driver's side bank (cylinders 4-6 on a US-market LHD car), and cylinder 6 is the one most commonly quoted as the first to go because it sits furthest from the oil pump and runs hottest. Photograph each bore and label the image by cylinder number.

torque.note: New plugs 30 Nm (22 ft-lb). Anti-seize is not required on the OE plug.

children.title: Leakdown and compression test, record per cylinder
children.notes: Warm engine, all plugs out, throttle propped open. Record both absolute numbers and cylinder-to-cylinder spread — spread matters more than absolute. Listen at the oil filler (rings), the intake (intake valve), the exhaust (exhaust valve) and the coolant tank (head gasket / D-chunk crack). Bubbles in the expansion tank during leakdown on one specific cylinder is the classic D-chunk / cracked-liner tell. Write the numbers on the build sheet; they are your before/after proof.

title: Car preparation and fluid drain
notes: 996 Targa specific: the sliding glass roof adds weight high up and the rear glass hatch is fragile — park the roof in the closed position and do not lean on the hatch. Disconnect the battery (front trunk, under the carpet on the left) and wait 15 minutes before touching anything electrical; note the radio code first. Get the car high enough on a four-post or on tall stands that a transmission jack plus the engine/trans assembly can roll out from under it — you need roughly 24 in / 600 mm of clearance under the rear.

torque.note: Applies to all 996 variants.

children.title: Drain engine oil, coolant, transmission oil; discharge A/C
children.notes: A/C MUST be discharged and recovered by a licensed shop before the condenser/compressor lines are opened — venting R134a is illegal. The 996 cooling system holds a lot of coolant and it does not all come out of the radiator drains; open the bleeder on the expansion tank and pull the lower hose at the thermostat housing. Expect to chase residual coolant for a while. Catch and measure what comes out so you know what to put back.

torque.note: New crush washer.
Open the FILL plug first — if you cannot open it, do not drain.

children.title: Remove rear bumper cover, undertrays, exhaust and rear wheels
children.notes: Rear bumper cover comes off after the tail light surround fasteners and the wheel-well liner screws; it is held by long horizontal guide rails — pull it straight back, not down. Photograph the position of the bumper shims. Expect several broken plastic clips; buy a clip assortment in advance. Soak every exhaust fastener in penetrant the night before — 20-year-old muffler-to-cat nuts snap as a matter of routine.

title: Disconnect all engine and transmission interfaces
notes: On a 996 the engine and transmission come out DOWNWARD as one assembly on the rear subframe/carrier — nothing comes out the top. Everything that crosses the plane between the body and the drivetrain has to be freed: fuel supply/return, coolant hoses, A/C lines, wiring harness plugs, shift cables, clutch slave hydraulic line, throttle cable/DBW connector, and the rear axle shafts. Work methodically bay-left to bay-right and bag-and-tag every fastener by location. Photograph each connector before unplugging it.

children.title: Relieve fuel pressure, disconnect fuel lines, harness and grounds
children.notes: Relieve rail pressure before opening any fuel fitting, and plug both lines immediately — the 996 will dribble a surprising amount. The main engine harness plug sits on the left side of the engine; release the lever slowly, the connector body is brittle with age. Do not forget the two engine ground straps — a missed ground causes maddening no-start diagnostics later.

children.title: Disconnect coolant hoses, A/C lines and heater lines
children.notes: Cap every opened A/C fitting immediately with new O-rings ready for reassembly; moisture in the system means a new receiver/drier. Inspect the plastic coolant distribution pieces and the thermostat housing as they come off — these are the M96's own coolant weak points and they go brittle. Photograph the hose routing around the AOS, it is easy to get wrong on reassembly.

children.title: Disconnect axle shafts, shift cables and clutch slave cylinder
children.notes: The axle shaft inner CV bolts are 12-point M8 (triple-square/XZN) and they round off if the socket is not driven fully home — clean the heads with a pick first. Support each axle with wire once free so the CV boot is not stretched. Leave the clutch slave cylinder bolted to the bellhousing and unbolt it from the line, or better, unbolt the slave and hang it on the body so the hydraulic system stays sealed and does not need bleeding later.

torque.spec: NOT VERIFIED IN RESEARCH — consult factory manual
torque.note: Commonly quoted in the 80 Nm class for the M10 variant and ~45-50 Nm for M8; verify before assembly. Always use new bolts.

title: Drop the engine and transmission out the bottom
notes: This is the defining 996 operation: the whole drivetrain lowers out of the car from underneath. Build or buy a cradle/table that supports BOTH the sump and the transmission — a bare transmission jack under one point will let the assembly tip. Take the weight on the cradle BEFORE undoing the engine and transmission mounts, then lower in small increments while a second person watches every remaining cable, hose and harness for tension. Budget 6 hours for a careful first-timer; an experienced shop quotes 4-6. Do not work alone on this step.

torque.fastener: Engine mount to carrier, upper bolts

tools: drivetrain drop table or two transmission jacks

children.title: Take the weight and lower the engine/transmission assembly out
children.notes: Take the full weight on the cradle BEFORE undoing the engine and transmission mounts. Then lower in small increments while a second person watches every remaining cable, hose and harness for tension — something is always still attached. An experienced shop quotes 4-6 hours for the drop; budget 6 for a careful first time. Do not attempt this alone, and do not let the assembly hang on one support point.

torque.fastener: Engine mount to carrier, upper bolts

tools: drivetrain drop table or two transmission jacks

children.title: Separate transmission from engine
children.notes: Pull the transmission straight back off the dowels — do NOT let it hang on the input shaft, that bends the clutch disc hub and can damage the guide tube. Support the transmission on its own stand. With the bellhousing open, inspect the clutch face, the release bearing and the guide tube, and look for oil: oil on the clutch from the engine side means a leaking RMS; from the transmission side means the input shaft seal.
tools: long extensions and swivels for bellhousing bolts

children.title: Remove clutch, pressure plate and dual-mass flywheel
children.notes: Lock the flywheel before loosening. Loosen the pressure plate bolts in a star pattern a turn at a time so the cover does not distort. The DMF is heavy — do not let it drop on the crank flange or the dowel. Before discarding, check the DMF: rotational free play (rock the secondary mass against the primary), radial rock, and any rattling or evidence of grease thrown out past the seal. Porsche/LuK spec a diagnostic tool for this; if in doubt on a 20-year-old car with the engine already out, replace it. THE FLYWHEEL BOLTS ARE TORQUE-TO-YIELD AND MUST NOT BE REUSED.

torque.note: TTY — new bolts mandatory. Torque-then-angle; use a proper angle gauge, not a guess.

children.title: Mount engine on a stand with an M96 adapter plate
children.notes: A generic four-arm stand will NOT bolt to an M96 — you need the bellhousing-pattern adapter plate. Use a stand rated well above the ~200 kg engine and put the stand on a solid floor; you will be applying real torque to this thing later. Mount it so the engine can rotate to put the case-half seam horizontal. Fit blanking plates/tape over every open port so nothing falls inside.

title: Strip external accessories, intake and exhaust from the engine
notes: Work top-down and keep hardware in labelled bags by assembly. Photograph the intake runner and vacuum routing before anything moves — the 996 3.6 resonance/intake plumbing is not intuitive on reassembly. Bag every sensor with its connector orientation photographed.

children.title: Remove intake manifold, throttle body, injectors and fuel rail
children.notes: Pull the fuel rail with the injectors attached, then press the injectors out. Every injector gets new upper and lower O-rings — they are hard as plastic at this age and they are a classic post-rebuild fuel-smell/rough-idle cause. Cover the head intake ports immediately. Inspect the intake ports for oil pooling: heavy oil in the intake is your AOS telling you it has failed.

torque.spec: NOT VERIFIED IN RESEARCH — low value, ~10 Nm class
torque.note: New throttle body gasket 996-110-317-52. Verify against factory manual.

children.title: Remove alternator, A/C compressor, power steering pump, belt drive, AOS, water pump
children.notes: The AOS and its vent hoses come off as a unit — replace all of it, the hoses go brittle and crack and a vacuum leak there is a genuine engine-killer (it can hydro-lock or run the engine on its own oil). The water pump almost certainly has a plastic impeller; replace it with a metal-impeller unit on principle, because a shed plastic impeller distributes itself through the whole cooling system. Inspect the accessory belt tensioner and idler bearings by hand — any roughness, replace.

torque.note: New O-ring/gasket; do not over-torque into the aluminium case.

children.title: Remove exhaust manifolds, heat shields and O2 sensors
children.notes: Heat and penetrant, then patience. Plan on snapping at least one manifold stud and plan the extraction in advance (weld a nut on rather than drill, if you can get to it). Remove the O2 sensors with a slotted sensor socket and do not hang them by their wires. All manifold gaskets and nuts are one-time-use.

torque.spec: NOT VERIFIED IN RESEARCH — consult factory manual
torque.note: Use new copper-plated lock nuts and new gaskets; anti-seize the studs on assembly.

torque.spec: NOT VERIFIED IN RESEARCH — typically 45-55 Nm class
torque.note: Never install an O2 sensor with anti-seize on the sensing tip.

title: Remove the IMS flange and rear main seal — identify the IMS bearing
notes: THE CENTRAL M96 DECISION POINT. On a 2003 996 3.6 (M96.03) the intermediate shaft bearing is, by model year, the SINGLE-ROW serviceable bearing. Identification, in order of reliability: (1) pull the flange and look — a single row of balls in a narrow race, with a comparatively wide flange; (2) measure the flange dish depth, quoted at 19.27 mm for single-row versus 13.34 mm for the dual-row; (3) cross-check the engine number stamped on the lower edge of the crankcase. Do NOT assume from the model year alone on an engine that may have been replaced under warranty — a swapped-in later engine could be a different variant. The large NON-SERVICEABLE bearing belongs to MY2006-2008 engines and cannot be replaced without splitting the case; since you are splitting the case anyway on this build, that would be an option rather than a disaster, but it is not what a 2003 should have. Photograph the bearing in situ before it moves, photograph the grease/debris state, and bag the old bearing as evidence.

torque.spec: NOT VERIFIED IN RESEARCH — consult LN/factory instructions
torque.note: The LN retrofit kit ships its own torque values; follow the kit instructions over any generic figure.

tools: LN IMS Retrofit tool 106-08.2.2 (purchase or rental)

children.title: Remove the IMS flange and positively identify the bearing variant
children.notes: Identify in this order of reliability: (1) pull the flange and look — a single row of balls in a narrow race with a comparatively wide flange; (2) measure flange dish depth, 19.27 mm for single-row versus 13.34 mm for dual-row; (3) cross-check the engine number stamped on the lower edge of the crankcase. Do NOT rely on model year alone — a warranty-replacement engine could be a different variant. Record the answer on the build sheet before you order any IMS part.

torque.spec: NOT VERIFIED IN RESEARCH — consult LN/factory instructions
torque.note: The LN kit ships its own torque values; those supersede any generic figure.

children.title: Inspect and document IMS bearing condition and shaft play
children.notes: Before the bearing comes out, feel for radial and axial play at the shaft nose. Any detectable play, any roughness on rotation, or a collapsed/missing seal on the outer race means the bearing has been shedding into the oil — which changes the whole build, because that debris has been through every bearing in the engine. Capture the state of the grease: a dry, brown, varnished bearing is the textbook pre-failure condition. Photograph the balls and both races.

children.title: Remove rear main seal and crankshaft flange area
children.notes: The RMS is the 996's most over-blamed and most misunderstood leak. LN's position is worth repeating: RMS leaks are not caused by the weight of the dual-mass flywheel, they come from case/block mis-machining at the factory or from an engine never updated to the current PTFE seal. Note carefully whether the old seal sat square in its bore. A PTFE seal is installed DRY — no oil, no grease on the lip — and must go in square with the proper tool, never tapped in with a socket.

title: Valvetrain, cam housings and timing drive teardown
notes: Before anything rotates or comes apart, set the engine to TDC cylinder 1 and mark the relationship of every sprocket to its chain with paint. Even though you will re-time from scratch with tooling, the marks tell you where the engine actually WAS, which is how you confirm a suspected timing slip. Keep every lifter, every cam follower and every valve in a labelled tray by exact position — used parts must go back in the same bore.

children.title: Remove cam covers, set TDC and lock the camshafts
children.notes: Photograph the VarioCam Plus solenoid positions and their wiring before removal. 2003 3.6 SPECIFIC: this is a VarioCam Plus engine — variable timing via an electro-hydraulic rotary vane adjuster at the nose of each INTAKE camshaft, plus two-stage valve lift via switchable tappets. It is NOT the earlier 3.4's chain-tensioner-actuated VarioCam. Note also that the 3.6 M96.03 is a THREE-chain engine (crank-to-IMS plus one chain per bank), where the 1999-2001 3.4 is a five-chain engine — the parts and the timing procedure are not interchangeable.
tools: cam locking/timing fixture (Porsche 9595-series or equivalent aftermarket P253 type)

children.title: Remove chain tensioners, chains, guide rails and chain ramps
children.notes: THE OTHER SIGNATURE M96 WEAR ITEM. The chain ramps and guides are plastic over a steel spine, and they heat-cycle themselves brittle then wear through — which retards cam timing and throws the deviation codes you logged at the start. Lay every ramp out and photograph the wear faces next to a new one; grooves worn past roughly half the pad thickness, or any cracking/missing chunks, condemn the set. ALL ramps, rails and chains get replaced on a full rebuild — they are cheap relative to doing this job twice. Retrieve the tensioner shoes and count the pieces; a missing chunk of ramp is somewhere in your engine and you need to find it.

torque.spec: NOT VERIFIED IN RESEARCH — consult factory manual
torque.note: Tensioners are hydraulic; they must be compressed and pinned on assembly, never installed pumped up.

torque.fastener: M6 x 30 pan-head socket screws at chain box (10.9)
torque.note: Use a magnetic bit for the screw that enters the slot — if dropped it goes into the crankcase.

children.title: Remove cam housings, camshafts and hydraulic lifters
children.notes: Loosen cam housing/bearing fasteners progressively in reverse of the tightening sequence, a little at a time across the whole housing, so the cam is not bent by uneven spring load. DO NOT use a magnet to lift the lifters out — there is a service bulletin against it because magnetising a hydraulic lifter makes it collect ferrous debris for the rest of its life. Use a suction tool or a lifter grabber. 3.6 SPECIFIC LIFTER SPLIT: the 2002-2008 3.6 uses 12 conventional non-variable lifters in the EXHAUST positions (996-105-041-72) and 12 switchable variable-lift lifters in the INTAKE positions (996-105-255-25) — they are different parts at very different prices, do not mix them up.

torque.fastener: Camshaft bearing housing / cam cap bolts
torque.spec: NOT VERIFIED IN RESEARCH — consult factory manual
torque.note: Must be tightened progressively in the specified sequence.

children.title: Remove cylinder heads
children.notes: The M96 is a long-bolt engine: the cylinder head fasteners are long through-bolts that pass through the head and clamp into the crankcase/crankshaft carrier, not short bolts into a deck. Loosen them in reverse sequence in several passes. The OEM through-bolts are TORQUE-TO-YIELD and must be discarded — this is where most builders switch to ARP studs (kit 204-4707) or Raceware. With the heads off, examine the head gasket fire rings for blow-by paths and the coolant ports for corrosion, and photograph both head gaskets in place before lifting them.

torque.spec: Reverse of tightening sequence, in stages
torque.note: OEM bolts are TTY, single use. Discard.

title: Bottom end teardown — oil system, case split, rotating assembly
notes: From here on, cleanliness discipline starts. Every part that comes off gets labelled by position. Two people and about 14 hours is a realistic figure for a full careful teardown from cam covers to bare case halves.

children.title: Remove sump/oil pan, pickup, oil pump and scavenge pumps
children.notes: Expect the sump to have been sealed with a heavy hand of Loctite 5900 — scrape it carefully and do not gouge the aluminium sealing face, and do not let scrapings fall into the case. Inspect the oil pump gears for scoring and measure gear-to-housing clearance. Check the oil pump drive — the OEM drive is a known weak link and a chromoly replacement is a sensible upgrade while you are in here. Inspect the pickup screen for the same debris you found in the filter.

torque.spec: NOT VERIFIED IN RESEARCH — consult factory manual
torque.note: Low value into aluminium; torque in a spiral sequence from the centre out.

children.title: Split the crankcase halves
children.notes: Mark the sealant bead line on the flange with a sharpie BEFORE you clean anything — the factory bead path is specific and you will want to reproduce it. Remove every case fastener (the M96.03 uses on the order of 25 case bolts plus 14 crankshaft carrier bolts) and lay them out on a board in a map of their positions; they are not all the same length. Separate the halves with even prying at the designated pry points ONLY — never between the sealing faces, a nick in that flange is a permanent oil leak. Split with the 1-3 half down and the 4-6 half up so the crank stays supported; use temporary bolts to support the crankshaft carrier as the halves come apart.

torque.spec: NOT VERIFIED IN RESEARCH — consult factory manual
torque.note: Multiple sizes and lengths; map them by position on removal.

torque.spec: NOT VERIFIED IN RESEARCH — consult factory manual or ARP instructions
torque.note: OEM are TTY. Rebuild kits commonly substitute ARP carrier bolts, which have their own published torque.

children.title: Remove crankshaft, connecting rods and pistons
children.notes: Measure crankshaft end play BEFORE disassembly and write it down — a rebuilt engine should come back in the middle of the spec range (one documented rebuild measured 0.004 in / 0.10 mm). Number every rod and cap to its journal and keep caps with their own rods; they are fracture-split and not interchangeable. GEOMETRY NOTE that catches people out on reassembly: pistons 1-3 come out and go back through the top of the bore normally, but 4-6 have to be passed through an access opening in the case wall with the rods still on the crank. Keep each piston with its bore and mark its orientation arrow. Bag the bearing shells by position — reading the wear pattern later is how you diagnose oiling problems.

torque.spec: NOT VERIFIED IN RESEARCH — consult factory manual or ARP instructions
torque.note: OEM are TTY and single use. Most rebuild kits supply ARP rod bolts; use ARP's published torque and ARP Ultra-Torque lubricant, not engine oil.

title: Inspection and measurement of every component
notes: Build a spreadsheet before you start measuring and fill it in as you go: every bore at three heights and two axes, every journal, every clearance. This record is what tells you whether you are doing a refresh or a full machining job, and it is the document you will want in five years. Photograph everything you measure next to the measuring instrument.

children.title: Cylinder bore inspection for scoring, taper and out-of-round
children.notes: THE DEFINING M96 INSPECTION. With the pistons out you can finally see the bottom of the bore where scoring starts and where the borescope could not reach. Look at the thrust faces. Vertical scoring you can catch a fingernail in is terminal for that bore. Documented rebuild practice: measure out-of-round perpendicular to the crank axis, with 0.0015 in quoted as a practical limit. Measure taper top to bottom. Cylinder 6 gets the most attention in the field — furthest from the oil pump, hottest, and the most commonly reported first failure — but check all six and do not stop at the first bad one. Inspect the piston skirts at the same time: flaking of the iron/ferrous coating off the skirt is the mechanism that starts the scoring. If any bore is scored, the honest answer is sleeving the whole block, not one hole.

children.title: Crankcase inspection — D-chunk cracks, sleeve integrity, bearing bores
children.notes: The D-chunk failure is a crack that propagates from the cylinder outward into the coolant passage, letting coolant flood the engine internals — it is the end state of untreated bore scoring, and it is reported most often on the 3.4 but is not exclusive to it. Inspect the outside of each cylinder from inside the case for cracks, and look for a slipped or cracked factory sleeve. Dye-penetrant or magnaflux the case if there is any doubt. Also check the main bearing bore alignment and roundness with the halves bolted together to spec, and inspect the case for the fretting and mis-machining that causes chronic RMS leaks. A block with cracked or slipped sleeves needs repair sleeves or replacement — decide here, not later.

children.title: Crankshaft, rod and bearing inspection
children.notes: Mic every main and rod journal in two axes at three points for taper and out-of-round. Check crank runout on V-blocks. Read the old bearing shells like a diagnostic: even grey wear is normal; copper showing through is overload or oil starvation; embedded glitter is the IMS bearing debris that has been circulating. Documented finding worth knowing — rod bearing 6 commonly shows the heaviest thrust-face wear, consistent with being furthest from the oil pump. Check rod big-end bore roundness and rod straightness; have rods resized if outside spec.

children.title: Cylinder head, valve and valve guide inspection
children.notes: Check head flatness with a straightedge and feelers in both diagonals and lengthwise. Measure valve stem-to-guide clearance by rocking each valve in its guide with a dial indicator — worn guides are common at this mileage and are a real oil-consumption source that people misattribute to rings or the AOS. Inspect the seats for recession and pitting, check for cracks between the valve seats and around the plug hole, and pressure-test the head if there is any sign of coolant intrusion. Check the cam bearing surfaces in the head/housing for scoring.

title: Machine shop operations
notes: Most of this is bench time for someone else, but your setup, spec sheet and QC on return are the hours that count. Send the shop a written spec: target bore, piston-to-wall clearance from the piston supplier, deck height, ring end gaps required, and the head gasket thickness you intend to run. Those choices are interdependent and the shop cannot guess them. Inspect and re-measure everything yourself when it comes back, before it goes anywhere near assembly.

children.title: Case machining, sleeving (Nickies) and decking
children.notes: If the bores are scored, the accepted repair on an M96 is to machine the case and install billet aluminium nickel-silicon-carbide plated cylinders (Nickies) with matched oversize forged pistons. NEVER use a steel sleeve in an M96 — the thermal expansion mismatch against the aluminium case is exactly the wrong answer and the industry consensus is unambiguous about it. Budget roughly USD 5,000-6,000 for case machining plus Nickies plus oversize forged pistons. The case halves must be align-bored/honed as a matched pair if the main bores are out. Decide bore size (96 mm stock, or 102/104 mm big-bore) before machining, because it sets the piston, ring and head gasket choice.
tools: machine shop: CNC boring, align hone, decking fixture

children.title: Cylinder head rebuild — valve job, guides, resurface
children.notes: Specify a three-angle valve job, new guides where clearance is out, new valve stem seals throughout, and a light resurface only if needed — remember the M96 head sits on a long-bolt stack, so material removed from the head changes the clamped stack height and interacts with head gasket thickness. Have the shop pressure-test both heads. Lap and vacuum-test each valve on return and photograph the seat contact rings.

children.title: Crankshaft polish/grind and rotating assembly balance
children.notes: Polish journals if within spec, grind undersize only if you must (and buy matching undersize bearings). Have the full rotating assembly — crank, rods, pistons, pins, rings, bearings, and the flywheel/clutch if you want it perfect — balanced as a set. This is the difference between a rebuilt engine and a built one, and on a flat-six it is felt directly in how the engine revs.

title: Bottom end assembly
notes: Stop. Before a single part goes together: clean every oil gallery with rifle brushes and solvent, blow out with filtered air, and cap them. Lay out a clean bench, wear nitrile gloves, and have all torque specs and the sealant on hand before you start — some of the sealant steps are on a clock and you cannot go looking for a wrench mid-bead.

children.title: Final clean, deburr and dry-fit the case halves
children.notes: Both sealing flanges must be perfectly clean and perfectly dry — any oil film and the sealant will not bond. Final wipe with brake cleaner or acetone on a lint-free cloth, then do not touch the flange with bare hands. Chase every threaded hole with a thread chaser (not a cutting tap) and blow out the chips. Dry-assemble the halves once with the crank in, without sealant, to confirm nothing binds and everything clears.

children.title: Install main bearings, crankshaft and check clearances
children.notes: Install bearing shells dry into clean saddles with the tangs located, then check clearance with Plastigage on every main before lubricating anything. When the numbers are confirmed, strip it, lubricate the shells with assembly lube and set the crank in. Set and verify crankshaft end play with the thrust bearings — aim for the middle of the spec range, not the edge. Record every number.

torque.spec: NOT VERIFIED IN RESEARCH — consult factory manual or ARP instructions
torque.note: 14 off. OEM TTY; ARP replacements have their own torque and require ARP lubricant.

children.title: Fit rings to pistons, install pistons and rods
children.notes: File-fit every ring: square each ring in its own bore with a piston and measure the end gap against the piston supplier's spec, not a generic figure. Stagger the ring gaps per the supplier's diagram. Use a TAPERED SLEEVE ring compressor, which is what the cylinder design wants — not a band-type compressor. Protect the rod bolts with hose sleeves so nothing touches the crank or the bore. THE 4-6 TRICK: pistons 4-6 must be fed in through the case access opening with the rods already on the crank. Do a dry practice run, use an alignment tool, and verify EVERY wrist pin circlip with a borescope after installation — a circlip that pops out destroys the engine.

torque.spec: NOT VERIFIED IN RESEARCH — consult factory manual or ARP instructions
torque.note: 12 off. OEM TTY, single use. With ARP bolts use ARP Ultra-Torque lubricant and ARP's published torque/stretch, and measure bolt stretch if you can.

children.title: Install the IMS bearing solution
children.notes: FOR A 2003 3.6, THE CHOICE IS BETWEEN TWO SINGLE-ROW PRODUCTS. (a) IMS Retrofit Single Row Pro (LN 106-08.2.2, around USD 999): a ceramic-hybrid ball bearing, serviceable, replaceable at clutch intervals, installable with the engine in the car. (b) IMS Solution Single Row (around USD 1,899): a pressure-fed PLAIN bearing — no balls, no rollers — which backdates the design to what Porsche used in the Mezger engines, carries no scheduled replacement interval and a 5-year unlimited-mileage warranty. WITH THE ENGINE ALREADY OUT AND THE CASE ALREADY APART, THE SOLUTION IS THE RATIONAL CHOICE — its installation requirements (oil feed provisions, full access) are free at this point in the build, and you never open this up again. Do not buy the Dual Row Pro for this engine unless you have physically confirmed a dual-row flange. Follow LN's kit instructions exactly; their torque values supersede any generic figure.

torque.note: Follow the supplied instructions, not a generic figure.

tools: LN IMS tool 106-08.2.2 (purchase or LN rental program)

children.title: Join the case halves — the sealant procedure
children.notes: THE HIGHEST-STAKES FIVE MINUTES OF THE BUILD. Have every bolt cleaned, laid out in its mapped position, and every tool in hand before you open the sealant. Porsche specifies Loctite 5900 flange sealant (Porsche PN 000-043-204-35, 50 ml). Many experienced M96 builders prefer Drei Bond 1209 instead, on the grounds that 5900 is messy and tends to squeeze debris into the block — either is defensible, but do not mix them. Apply a thin, continuous, even bead following the marked path (mark the line with a sharpie beforehand, per the manual illustration); too much sealant is far worse than too little because the excess goes INSIDE the engine and ends up in the oil pickup. You have roughly a five-minute working window before cure begins. Bring the halves together square, start every bolt by hand, then torque in the specified sequence in stages. Do not rotate the crank until the sealant has cured.

torque.spec: NOT VERIFIED IN RESEARCH — consult factory manual
torque.note: Multiple lengths and diameters, tightened in a specified sequence in stages. Install new O-rings on the through-bolts.

title: Top end assembly, timing and cam timing
notes: Cleanliness rules still apply. Everything here is sequence-critical; do not improvise the order.

children.title: Install oil pump, pickup and sump
children.notes: Prime the oil pump with assembly lube before it goes on so it can pull oil on first crank. New pickup tube O-ring — a leak here is an air leak that starves the engine and is invisible from outside. Consider the chromoly oil pump drive upgrade now, it is inaccessible later. Seal the sump with a thin even bead; the previous builder's excess 5900 is why you spent an hour scraping.

torque.spec: NOT VERIFIED IN RESEARCH — consult factory manual
torque.note: Spiral sequence from centre out, in stages.

children.title: Install cylinder heads and torque the long bolts
children.notes: New head gaskets (996-104-201-04), fitted dry unless the gasket maker says otherwise, and correctly oriented. Oil the threads and the underside of the bolt heads per the manual. THE FACTORY 996 3.6 SEQUENCE IS UNUSUAL — READ IT TWICE: tighten all bolts to 30 Nm in the specified sequence, then UNDO ALL THE SCREWS AGAIN, then tighten to 20 Nm in sequence, then final tighten with 2 x 70 degrees of torque angle. The deliberate loosen-and-retighten step is not a typo and it is the step people skip. If you are running ARP 204-4707 studs instead, follow ARP's procedure — 60 ft-lb final in two equal steps using ARP Ultra-Torque assembly lubricant, NOT engine oil, because the lubricant is what makes the preload repeatable.

torque.spec: 30 Nm (22 ft-lb) in sequence, then undo all; 20 Nm (15 ft-lb) in sequence; then 2 x 70 deg angle
torque.note: TTY — new bolts mandatory. Do not substitute the M96/70 Mezger procedure (which is 30 Nm, undo, 20 Nm, then 120 deg) — different engine, different spec.

torque.spec: 60 ft-lb (81 Nm) final, in two equal steps
torque.note: Use ARP Ultra-Torque fastener assembly lubricant, not motor oil. Studs are reusable, unlike the OEM TTY bolts.

torque.fastener: M6 x 30 pan-head socket screws (10.9) at chain box
torque.note: Use a magnetic bit holder for the screw entering the slot — if dropped it falls into the crankcase.

tools: beam or click torque wrench 20-150 Nm

children.title: Install lifters, camshafts and cam housings
children.notes: Soak new hydraulic lifters in clean oil and keep them upright. Remember the 3.6 split: switchable variable-lift lifters (996-105-255-25) go in the INTAKE positions, conventional lifters (996-105-041-72) in the EXHAUST positions. Lubricate cam lobes and journals with assembly lube. Torque the cam housing fasteners progressively and evenly in the specified sequence so the camshaft is never bent by uneven spring load.

torque.spec: NOT VERIFIED IN RESEARCH — consult factory manual
torque.note: Progressive, sequenced tightening in several passes.

children.title: Install timing chains, guide rails, ramps and tensioners
children.notes: All new ramps, rails and chains — this is not the place to reuse. New O-rings on every ramp bolt, and clean and lightly grease the bolts as you go. The 3.6 is a three-chain layout: crank-to-IMS, plus one chain per bank. Compress and pin the hydraulic tensioners before installing them; never fit a pumped-up tensioner. Consider the billet IMS chain tensioner paddle upgrade in place of the plastic original. Verify every rail is fully seated and every retaining pin is captured before the covers go on.

torque.spec: NOT VERIFIED IN RESEARCH — consult factory manual
torque.note: Tensioners must be compressed/pinned before installation and released only after the chain is routed.

children.title: Set camshaft timing and verify deviation
children.notes: THE STEP THAT DECIDES WHETHER THE ENGINE LIVES. Bring the engine to TDC cylinder 1 on the compression stroke and lock it there. Fit the cam holding/locking fixtures to both banks (Porsche 9595-series tooling or a competent aftermarket equivalent such as the P253 type). Time the chains, release the tensioners, then rotate the engine through at least two full turns BY HAND — if anything binds, stop and find out why before you apply any more force. Re-check TDC and re-verify the locks still drop in. A widely used belt-and-braces practice among M96 builders is red thread locker on the cam sprocket bolts as insurance against timing slip. Finally, after first start, read camshaft deviation for both banks with a scan tool and compare against the values you logged at the very beginning — that is the closed loop on the whole job.

torque.spec: NOT VERIFIED IN RESEARCH — consult factory manual
torque.note: Red (high-strength) thread locker is common practice here as anti-slip insurance.

tools: Porsche 9595-series cam holding fixture / P253-type timing lock tool
Durametric or PIWIS for deviation readout

title: Close up the engine — seals, flywheel, clutch and accessories
notes: Last chance to catch anything before the engine goes back under the car. Do a written checklist walk-around: every fastener torqued and marked, every plug fitted, every sensor connected.

children.title: Install the rear main seal and front crankshaft seal
children.notes: Use the current genuine Porsche PTFE rear main seal (0PB-105-249) — it is the updated design and it is what fixes the chronic leak history. INSTALL IT DRY: no oil, no grease, nothing on the lip. It must go in square and to the correct depth, which means the Porsche 9699 + 9699/2 tool or the LN equivalent (0PB.105.249.LN). Do not tap it in with a socket and do not touch the sealing lip with your fingers.

children.title: Install dual-mass flywheel, clutch and release bearing
children.notes: NEW TTY FLYWHEEL BOLTS, no exceptions — the OEM bolts stretch by design and are single-use. Torque 25 Nm then 90 degrees with a proper angle gauge. Centre the clutch disc with an alignment tool before final-torquing the pressure plate, and tighten the cover bolts in a star pattern in stages. Fit the new release bearing and check the guide tube for wear. Photograph the assembly before the transmission goes on.

torque.note: TTY — new bolts mandatory.

torque.spec: NOT VERIFIED IN RESEARCH — consult factory manual
torque.note: Star pattern, in stages.

children.title: Refit water pump, AOS, accessories, intake and exhaust manifolds
children.notes: Metal-impeller water pump, new thermostat, all new AOS hoses, new injector O-rings, new exhaust manifold gaskets and nuts with anti-seize on the studs. Fit all sensors and route the harness exactly as photographed at teardown. Fit new spark plugs and inspect the coils — 20-year-old coils on a freshly rebuilt engine is a false economy.

torque.note: Reused plugs 25 Nm (19 ft-lb).

title: Reinstall engine and transmission in the car
notes: Essentially the drop in reverse, and it goes faster — but the risk of damaging a new engine is highest here. Mate the transmission to the engine on the bench/cradle, on the dowels, without forcing. Raise the assembly slowly and keep checking clearance to the body, the coolant pipes and the A/C lines. New motor mounts and transmission mount while it is all apart; 20-year-old rubber under a fresh engine is not worth the hours to do again.

torque.fastener: Engine mount to carrier, upper bolts

children.title: Mate transmission to engine and lift the assembly into the car
children.notes: Mate the transmission to the engine on the cradle, onto the dowels, without forcing — never pull it together with the bellhousing bolts. Raise the assembly slowly, checking clearance to the body, coolant plumbing and A/C lines continuously. This is where the risk of damaging a brand-new engine is highest, so go slowly and use a second set of eyes.

torque.fastener: Engine mount to carrier, upper bolts

children.title: Reconnect fuel, coolant, electrical, A/C, shifter and axles
children.notes: Work from the photographs. New O-rings on every A/C joint and have the system evacuated and recharged professionally. New crush washers/O-rings on fuel fittings. Double-check both engine ground straps. Before you fill anything, do a connector audit against your teardown photos — a single unplugged sensor will have you chasing a phantom for an evening.

torque.spec: NOT VERIFIED IN RESEARCH — consult factory manual
torque.note: New bolts. Clean the 12-point heads before seating the socket.

tools: A/C vacuum pump and gauges (shop service)

children.title: Fill fluids and bleed the cooling system
children.notes: Engine oil: approximately 8.25 L (8.7 US qt) for an oil-and-filter change; approximately 10.25 L (10.8 US qt) for a completely dry fill, which is what you have now — fill to the dry-fill figure, then set the level properly on the dipstick/electronic gauge once it has run and settled. Use an oil meeting the Porsche A40 approval, typically a 0W-40 or 5W-40 full synthetic. BLEEDING THE 996 COOLING SYSTEM IS FIDDLY AND MATTERS: the engine is behind you and the radiators are at the front, with high points in between. Use the bleeder screw, run the heater on full hot, and expect to top up repeatedly over several heat cycles. An air pocket on a fresh engine is a very expensive way to learn this.

torque.note: New crush washer.

title: First start, break-in and validation
notes: The rebuild is not finished when it starts; it is finished when it has been validated. Have a fire extinguisher within reach and a second person watching for leaks during every one of these steps.

children.title: Prime the oil system before the first start
children.notes: Do not let a fresh engine fire on dry bearings. Disable ignition and fuel, then crank in short bursts until oil pressure registers. Confirm pressure before you allow it to start. Verify no fuel or coolant leaks while cranking.

children.title: First start and initial heat cycle
children.notes: Start it and bring it straight to a fast idle around 2000 rpm — do not let a fresh engine sit at low idle, the cam lobes and lifters want oil flow. Watch coolant temperature and oil pressure continuously. Listen for anything rhythmic. Let it reach operating temperature, then shut down and let it cool completely. Check for leaks at every joint you made, especially the case seam, the sump, the RMS and the head gaskets. Re-read camshaft deviation on both banks now and compare to your baseline.

children.title: Break-in driving and first oil change
children.notes: Follow the ring and cylinder supplier's break-in schedule — with Nickies or any specific piston/ring package, THEIR procedure overrides generic advice. Broadly: varied load and rpm, no sustained constant speed, no lugging, no full throttle for the first stage, and plenty of engine braking to load the rings against the bore. Change the oil and filter early (commonly in the 500-1000 mile window), then cut that filter open too — it is your first real report card on the build. Re-check coolant level at every cool-down, and re-torque anything the fastener supplier specifies a re-torque for (Raceware studs, for instance, require a documented re-torque after heat cycling).

torque.fastener: Head studs — re-torque if specified by the stud supplier
torque.note: Raceware require a mandatory re-torque after heat cycling; ARP 204-4707 as supplied do not call for one. Follow the instructions in your box.

children.title: Post break-in validation and documentation
children.notes: Close the loop on every measurement you took at the start: leakdown and compression on all six, camshaft deviation both banks, fuel trims, oil consumption over a measured interval, and a borescope of every bore. Photograph the filter media from the break-in oil change. File the complete build record — measurements, part numbers, torque log, machine shop invoices and photographs. On an M96 rebuild this documentation is worth real money at resale, because the first question any informed buyer asks is what was done about the IMS and the bores.
